meeting_header: Date: 2026-08-17, Start: 15:00 UTC, Duration: 64m. Attendees: Redwood (Sofia Park, Liam O'Connor, Miguel Reyes) / MeridianBank (Anita Patel, Jared Klein, Priya Sharma, Tom Wu). Recording: yes. Notes exported from Fireflies.ai.
summary: Deep-dive on private deployment hardening: isolation gateway design, ingress/egress controls, firewall patterns, KMS/HSM integration, RBAC/SSO mapping, and audit/log retention to satisfy SOC 2 and upcoming ISO audit. Customer required clear compensating controls for external egress and TLS inspection policy. Agreed next steps: send security pack, define pilot VPC, run latency/egress benchmarks, and confirm audit event list.
topics: Network isolation topology options (air-gapped vs controlled egress gateway)
Ingress patterns: ALB + TLS termination vs passthrough at perimeter
Egress control: proxy vs firewall vs policy-based routing
KMS/HSM integration and key custody models
RBAC, SSO, and least-privilege for control plane and console
Audit logs, retention, and evidence for SOC 2/ISO
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We'll focus on private deploy architecture and the isolation gateway patterns you asked for. Anita?
[00:08] Anita Patel: Thanks Sofia. We're short on time today so want to get to the egress question quickly — legal flagged data leaving the network, and our auditors want proof of controls.
[00:16] Liam O'Connor: Totally. We'll walk through a couple of topologies: fully isolated (air-gap-ish) with controlled data diode-style egress, and a VPC-based isolation with egress gateway/proxy and egress allow-listing.
[00:29] Jared Klein: Quick thing, we do need to maintain TLS termination in a way that doesn't break our DPI inspection. We currently do SNI-based inspection and enterprise TLS break-and-inspect via our proxy. How would Redwood's private control plane interact with that?
[00:42] Miguel Reyes: Great question. Two patterns: 1) TLS passthrough at the gateway all the way to the Redwood runtime inside your VPC — that preserves end-to-end TLS and your DPI sees the SNI only; 2) TLS termination at the egress gateway with internal mTLS to the runtime, which lets the gateway inspect plaintext then re-encrypt. Both have tradeoffs on observability and latency.
[01:02] Tom Wu: Passthrough is preferable from a compliance angle if we can't allow plaintext in the DMZ. But passthrough complicates things like L7 routing when you need to steer requests to different runtime clusters.
[01:16] Sofia Park: Right — latency and routing complexity are the core tradeoffs. We can support SNI routing with passthrough using SNI-based routing at the loadbalancer, or use TCP-level routing with consistent hashes. For our dedicated stacks we often recommend TLS passthrough if the customer's DPI policy forbids termination outside of a vetted enclave.
[01:33] Priya Sharma: On the audit side, we need immutable logs for every operator action, token issuance, and model version rollouts. Retention 7 years for certain artifacts. Do you store audit events locally in the control plane or stream them to our SIEM?
[01:45] Liam O'Connor: We ship audit events to a customer-configurable sink. For private deployments in a VPC we can push to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Log Collector or a secure S3 bucket (with server-side encryption). We also provide signed audit bundles for offline archiving for compliance evidence.
[02:00] Anita Patel: Signed audit bundles sounds useful. Can you sign with an HSM-backed key that we control?
[02:06] Miguel Reyes: Yes — you can bring your own key (BYOK) via KMS/HSM integration. The control plane supports using customer-managed KMS keys for encrypting persisted material and for signing audit artifacts. There are two modes: customer-managed KMS in the customer's account (preferred) or Redwood-managed HSM if needed for air-gapped installs.
[02:24] Jared Klein: For SOC 2 we also need RBAC tied to SSO. Can your console's RBAC map directly to our Okta groups? We need least privilege for operators and separate service accounts for CI.
[02:36] Sofia Park: Yes, we support SAML/SSO with SCIM group sync. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles and enforce MFA via your IdP. Service accounts are separate identities with scoped tokens and auditable actions.
[02:48] Tom Wu: Back to egress: how do you recommend preventing covert channels? We're worried about encoded exfil across allowed APIs.
[02:57] Liam O'Connor: Common controls: 1) strict allow-listing of DNS and IP destinations; 2) deep packet inspection or proxying for outbound HTTP(s); 3) per-model and per-route rate limits and data exfil detection rules; 4) egress NAT with justification logs. We can emit high-fidelity telemetry to your SIEM to detect anomalous patterns.
[03:18] Anita Patel: Is it possible to force all model downloads and artifact pulls through an internal artifact repository? We want to avoid any runtime outbound to public endpoints.
[03:26] Miguel Reyes: Absolutely — you can mirror models into a private registry or object store and lock down the runtime's network policies so the only allowed outbound is the registry endpoint and the KMS endpoint. That satisfies a lot of air-gap-style requirements while keeping manageability.
[03:41] Priya Sharma: For KMS, we need key rotation logs and separation of duties. Who has access to rotate keys?
[03:46] Liam O'Connor: Rotation happens in your KMS. Redwood will call KMS APIs using an IAM role. We recommend separation where security team retains key rotation privileges; Redwood's service account has encrypt/decrypt but not rotation unless explicitly granted. Rotation events are captured in the KMS audit logs which you own.
[03:59] Jared Klein: On firewalling, we run strict egress on the perimeter firewall. How granular are the IPs Redwood recommends? Is there a CIDR set we can lock down to?
[04:09] Sofia Park: For private deployments the runtime lives inside your VPC so there're no public IPs for the runtime. For any control-plane callbacks or metrics sinks, we can provide a small set of egress IP ranges or better, a static endpoint in your account (VPC endpoint) — then no external CIDR is needed.
[04:25] Tom Wu: OK, static endpoints preferred. What about the control plane — does it need persistent connectivity out to Redwood? Some of our policies require the control plane to be in a separate air-gapped subnet with only periodic admin syncs.
[04:37] Miguel Reyes: We support both continuous and batched-control modes. For highly restricted networks, the control plane can run in a customer-managed mode where telemetry and rollout calls are batched and sent via an approved egress window, or you can opt for a fully offline control plane that you manage entirely.
[04:52] Sofia Park: To be explicit: managed control plane inside your VPC gives you console + onboarding convenience. Self-managed/private control plane means you operate the control plane components; Redwood provides the artifacts and support.
[05:03] Anita Patel: About evidence for ISO — we need continuous integration proofs: how configurations are applied and drift detection for network policies. Can we get a policy-as-code export?
[05:14] Liam O'Connor: Yes, all config applied by our orchestration is represented as declarative manifests. We can export those manifests and provide diffs for rollouts. We also emit change events to your SCM or CI system for traceability.
[05:27] Jared Klein: A tangent, but do you have guidance for per-tenant encryption at rest? We want to ensure customer data and model cache segments are segregated.
transcript_continued:
[05:35] Miguel Reyes: We support tenant-level encryption scopes. Each tenant's artifacts and caches can be stored in separate prefixes with their own KMS keys. The runtime enforces namespace isolation and KV cache boundaries.
[05:47] Priya Sharma: Are there any known gotchas with instance metadata services? We need to ensure no inadvertent credential exposure.
[05:54] Liam O'Connor: Good call — recommend IMDSv2 only with metadata endpoint firewalling; service accounts are scoped and token lifetimes are short. For our images we strip build-time secrets and we recommend VM-level ephemeral creds where possible.
[06:07] Tom Wu: How is network policy enforced inside the node? Do you depend on security groups alone or use eBPF/iptables?
[06:13] Miguel Reyes: We typically rely on the cloud provider security groups + host-level iptables with a small userspace agent to enforce microsegmentation. For customers wanting stronger guarantees we can integrate with Cilium/eBPF for L7 policies.
[06:27] Sofia Park: Jumping forward to the mitigation for latency — if you terminate TLS at the gateway you add roughly X to Y ms depending on traffic and inspection rules; Liam will supply a short doc and numbers.
[06:38] Liam O'Connor: I'll run a test with TLS passthrough vs termination and show delta in median p50/p95. Also will test with KV cache hit/miss to demonstrate token latencies.
[06:48] Anita Patel: Regarding governance, we need role separation: who can push model updates to production? We need canary rollouts and rollback proofs.
[06:55] Miguel Reyes: Our rollout system supports RBAC-bound canary windows and auto-rollbacks on failure. All rollouts produce an immutable audit trail (who, what, when). We can tie rollout permissions to Okta groups.
[07:08] Priya Sharma: For long term retention we asked for 7-year signed logs; storage cost will be a consideration. Do you recommend compressed archives or cold-tier?
[07:17] Liam O'Connor: Use cold-tier encrypted storage with lifecycle rules. We also sign-manifest the bundles so the authenticity is preserved; you can keep a digest and store large blobs in glacier-equivalent.
[07:28] Jared Klein: For our internal firewall policy we'll want a one-page runbook that ops can follow for enabling/disabling egress allowances during a breach. Could Redwood provide a recommended playbook?
[07:36] Sofia Park: We have a hardened egress playbook template. We'll attach that to the security packet.
[07:41] Tom Wu: A few practicals: does the runtime need outbound DNS to 8.8.8.8? We want to avoid public resolvers in prod.
[07:48] Miguel Reyes: No — bind to your VPC resolver and we can pin DNS entries in the VPC. For model registries we recommend private endpoints or endpoint service in your account.
[07:58] Anita Patel: Ok one last thing — for the SOC 2 evidence, can we request on-demand export of operator sessions and console activity for a given time window?
[08:06] Liam O'Connor: Yes. We can export session logs, command audit trails, and signed artifacts for any timeframe. We'll also provide a mapping doc that tells you which event corresponds to which SOC control.
closing:
[08:20] Sofia Park: Great, recap: we'll send the security packet and diagram, Liam will bench TLS options, Anita to confirm egress allow-list, Meridan (Anita) to confirm audit retention fields. Aim to kick off pilot week of 2026-09-07. Thanks all.
[08:38] Miguel Reyes: I'll share the playbook and a short checklist for onboarding.
[08:45] Anita Patel: Thanks everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.
[08:49] Sofia Park: End call.
